opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The hand is the hardest part of a humanoid, and every choice about it is a trade-off.

The first question is how much dexterity you actually need. It's tempting to copy the human hand: five fingers, twenty-plus degrees of freedom, tendon-driven, with skin-like sensing everywhere. That looks great in a demo. But every extra joint adds an actuator, a sensor, and wiring to route through a very small space, and each one is another failure point. So we start from the task, not the anatomy. Moving totes in a warehouse, opening doors, carrying equipment, or operating tools built for human hands? Those tasks call for very different hands.

For business deployments, uptime and cost matter most. A customer doesn't care that the hand can do a party trick if it breaks every two hundred hours or costs as much as the rest of the robot. In practice that often means fewer actuated degrees of freedom, some underactuation so the fingers conform passively to an object, and a design where the fingers or the whole end effector can be swapped quickly in the field. Serviceability is a design requirement, not an afterthought.

For defense, robustness rises to the top. The hand has to survive dust, water, temperature extremes, shock, and rough handling. It may have to grip tools and equipment designed for a soldier in gloves. Grip strength and durability often matter more there than fine manipulation, and you have to handle degraded conditions. If a finger is damaged, the hand should still be useful rather than become a paperweight.

Then there's sensing versus simplicity. Tactile sensing is improving fast, and it makes learned manipulation policies much more capable, because the robot can feel slip, contact, and force instead of inferring everything from vision. But tactile skins are still fragile and expensive, so we place sensing where it pays off most: fingertips, the palm, and force/torque sensing at the wrist.

There's also a software angle that people underestimate. The hand design and the learning stack are coupled. If you train policies from human teleoperation or video, a more anthropomorphic hand makes it easier to transfer human demonstrations. A simpler gripper is more reliable but can make that mapping harder. So part of the trade-off is choosing which data pipeline you're betting on.

My general philosophy is to be as human-like as the job requires and no more. The humanoid form exists so the robot can work in spaces and with tools built for people, and the hand should serve that goal. But reliability, cost, and maintainability decide whether a robot ships in volume or stays a lab project.

r001.rationale: The response says defense hands may prioritize grip strength and durability, but does not compare strength needs with household chores or clearly identify this comparison as a design basis.

r002.rationale: It mentions wrist force/torque sensing and the space needed for wiring, but does not explain retaining hand-related components in the forearm to meet strength requirements.

r003.rationale: It refers to tools and equipment designed for human hands, but does not describe testing against customers’ actual physical equipment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the hand is where the robot's cost, reliability, and usefulness all collide, so you have to be honest about what jobs the thing is actually going to do.

The first trade-off is degrees of freedom versus robustness. A fully articulated five-finger hand with twenty-plus joints is impressive in a demo, but every joint is a motor, a tendon, a sensor, and a failure point. In a warehouse or on a flight line, a hand that works ninety-nine percent of the time with six or eight degrees of freedom beats a hand that does origami but needs servicing every week. So we ask: what fraction of the real tasks need true in-hand manipulation versus a good power grasp and a precision pinch? For most business cases it's a surprisingly small fraction.

The second is durability. Humanoid hands get banged into shelves, doors, and truck beds. In defense settings they get dirt, water, cold, and impacts. That pushes you toward underactuated designs where compliance is built into the mechanism, so a collision just deflects the fingers instead of stripping a gear. It also pushes you toward putting the actuators up in the forearm and running tendons, which keeps the hand light and cheap to replace. We treat the hand as a consumable, frankly.

Third is sensing. Tactile sensing is where the real capability unlock is, because it lets the AI close the loop on slip and contact rather than relying on vision alone. But sensors are also the first thing to fail. So the question is how much sensing gives you enough signal for learned policies without turning the hand into a fragile instrument.

And the last one is modularity. For business customers, the same robot might need a two-finger gripper one day and a dexterous hand the next. For defense, you might need a hand rated for a different environment or one that can hold a specific tool. A quick-change wrist interface with standard power and data means you don't design one perfect hand, you design a family and let the mission pick.

So my short answer is: start from the task distribution, build the simplest hand that covers most of it reliably, make it cheap enough to swap, and spend your complexity budget on sensing and software rather than on joints.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe testing hand capabilities against customers’ actual physical equipment.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the job you need the robot to do. A human hand is incredibly versatile, but recreating all of that capability adds complexity, cost, and things that can break. For a business, the question is whether that extra dexterity actually helps the robot do useful work reliably.

If you're moving boxes, you may need a robust gripper more than you need five fingers. If you're handling tools designed for people, then a more humanlike hand can make sense. Even then, you have to balance dexterity against grip strength, sensing, and how easily you can repair it.

For defense applications, I'd put even more emphasis on durability and maintenance. Can it work in dirt and rain? Can someone replace a damaged component quickly? The best hand isn't necessarily the one that looks most like ours. It's the one that consistently does the required task under the conditions where it will actually be used.

r001.rationale: The response mentions grip strength and durability for business and defense, but does not say those applications require greater hand strength than household chores.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that prioritizing strength motivates retaining hand-related components in the robot’s forearm.

r003.rationale: It discusses matching hands to tasks and tools, but does not describe testing against customers’ actual physical equipment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the job you’re asking the robot to do. A human hand is incredibly versatile, but replicating all of that capability adds mechanical complexity, cost, and things that can fail. The question is how much dexterity you actually need for the mission.

For a business application, that might mean handling tools, moving materials, or operating equipment designed for people. In defense, you also have to think about rough handling, dirt, weather, and whether somebody can repair it in the field. A very sophisticated hand isn’t useful if it’s constantly out of service.

So I’d work backward from the tasks. What does it need to grasp? How much force does it need? Does it need precise finger movements, or would a simpler, more durable gripper do the job? You want enough capability to be useful, with the reliability to keep doing that job.
